misconceptions.statement: A green light means I can cross without looking because all traffic must be stopped.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the colour as a guarantee rather than a signal others may break.
misconceptions.fix: Green means you may go, but you must still check for vehicles that jump the red or turn across your path.

probe.question: The pedestrian light turns green. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Walk straight across without looking.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule is always followed by everyone

misconceptions.statement: Yellow light means speed up to get through before it turns red.
misconceptions.why: Drivers around them often accelerate at amber to beat the red.
misconceptions.fix: Yellow means the signal is about to turn red, so slow down and stop unless you are too close to stop safely.

probe.question: The light turns yellow as you approach. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Speed up to cross before red.

misconceptions.root_belief: what people commonly do is the rule
misconceptions.source_hint: road safety studies of driver behaviour at signalised junctions

misconceptions.statement: Amber means the same as green, so you can go.
misconceptions.why: Amber is seen as a lighter version of go.
misconceptions.fix: Amber is a warning between green and red: prepare to stop.

probe.question: What does the amber light tell a driver?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep going as if it were green.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The shape of a road sign does not matter; only the picture counts.
misconceptions.why: Children look at the picture and ignore the border shape.
misconceptions.fix: Shape tells the type: circles give orders, triangles warn of danger, rectangles inform.

probe.question: A triangular sign shows a bend ahead. What type is it?
probe.wrong_answer: It is an order you must obey, like a circular sign.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the main detail matters, not the form

misconceptions.statement: Signs are only advice, so ignoring them is not an offence.
misconceptions.why: Students see people ignore signs without immediate consequence.
misconceptions.fix: Mandatory signs are legal rules, and breaking them is punishable by fine; warning and information signs help you drive safely.

probe.question: Is a 'No entry' sign just a suggestion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, you may enter if the road is empty.

misconceptions.root_belief: rules not enforced right now are optional

misconceptions.statement: At a zebra crossing, pedestrians can step out without checking because vehicles must always stop.
misconceptions.why: Students hear that pedestrians have right of way.
misconceptions.fix: Drivers should give way, but a fast vehicle cannot stop at once, so pedestrians must check and make eye contact before stepping.

probe.question: You reach a zebra crossing with a car approaching fast. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Walk out because the car must stop.

misconceptions.root_belief: having the right means being safe
misconceptions.source_hint: pedestrian safety studies on right-of-way assumptions

misconceptions.statement: It is safe to cross anywhere if I run fast.
misconceptions.why: Students overrate their own speed compared with vehicles.
misconceptions.fix: Cross at marked crossings, because drivers cannot judge or stop for a running child and running raises the risk of falling.

probe.question: No crossing nearby, a road is busy. Safe to run across?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if I run fast enough.

misconceptions.root_belief: my own speed can beat any danger

misconceptions.statement: Pedestrians should walk with the traffic on the road edge where there is no footpath.
misconceptions.why: Students think walking the same way as vehicles is natural.
misconceptions.fix: Where there is no footpath, walk on the right side facing oncoming traffic so you can see vehicles coming (in India, where traffic keeps left).

probe.question: No footpath on a village road. Which side should you walk?
probe.wrong_answer: Left side, with the traffic behind you.

misconceptions.root_belief: same direction as others is always safest

misconceptions.statement: Wearing a helmet loosely or unfastened still protects the head.
misconceptions.why: Students think owning or wearing it is enough.
misconceptions.fix: An unfastened helmet can fly off in a crash; it must be buckled and snug.

probe.question: A rider wears a helmet with the strap open. Is the head protected?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the helmet is on.

misconceptions.root_belief: having the object is enough without correct use

misconceptions.statement: Helmets are only for long highway trips, not short rides in the neighbourhood.
misconceptions.why: Danger is linked to distance and highways.
misconceptions.fix: Many crashes happen close to home at low speeds; a helmet should be worn on every ride.

probe.question: Do you need a helmet for a 5-minute ride to the shop?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a short trip.

misconceptions.root_belief: short or small exposure means small risk
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO road safety reports on crash locations

misconceptions.statement: Only the person driving the two-wheeler needs a helmet.
misconceptions.why: The driver is seen as the only one at risk.
misconceptions.fix: The pillion rider is just as likely to be thrown off and hit the head, so needs a helmet too.

probe.question: A father drives and his child sits behind. Who must wear a helmet?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the father.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the one in control is at risk

misconceptions.statement: Seatbelts are not needed when the car moves slowly.
misconceptions.why: Slow feels harmless.
misconceptions.fix: Even at city speeds the body keeps moving forward when the car stops suddenly, and the belt prevents hitting the dashboard.

probe.question: A car at 30 km/h brakes suddenly. Does a seatbelt matter?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is too slow to hurt.

misconceptions.root_belief: small numbers mean no real effect
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO seat-belt guidance and inertia misconception research

misconceptions.statement: In a crash, the car's airbag does the job of a seatbelt, so the belt is unnecessary.
misconceptions.why: Airbags are heavily advertised as safety devices.
misconceptions.fix: Airbags are designed to work together with seatbelts; without a belt, an airbag may not protect and can even injure.

probe.question: A car has airbags. Is a seatbelt needed?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the airbag is enough.

misconceptions.root_belief: one safety feature replaces all others
misconceptions.source_hint: vehicle safety guidance from road safety authorities

misconceptions.statement: Only front-seat passengers need to wear seatbelts.
misconceptions.why: People think the front is the dangerous place.
misconceptions.fix: Rear passengers without belts can be thrown forward and injure themselves and front-seat people.

probe.question: You sit in the back of a car. Do you need a belt?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the front seat needs it.

misconceptions.root_belief: danger is only where it is most visible
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO road safety reports on rear-seat belt use

misconceptions.statement: A small child is safest held in an adult's lap in the front seat.
misconceptions.why: Parents feel their arms are the safest place.
misconceptions.fix: An adult cannot hold a child in a crash; children should sit in the back in a proper child seat or belt.

probe.question: Where should a 3-year-old travel in a car?
probe.wrong_answer: On a parent's lap in front.

misconceptions.root_belief: personal strength can replace equipment

misconceptions.statement: Doubling the speed only doubles the danger of a crash.
misconceptions.why: Students assume linear growth.
misconceptions.fix: Crash energy grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed makes impact about four times as strong.

probe.question: A car at 40 km/h hits a wall versus 80 km/h. How much worse is the impact?
probe.wrong_answer: Twice as bad.

misconceptions.root_belief: effects grow in direct proportion to cause
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on proportional reasoning in kinetic energy

misconceptions.statement: Speed only matters when the driver is inexperienced; skilled drivers can go fast safely.
misconceptions.why: Students trust skill over physics.
misconceptions.fix: Skill does not change physics; at high speed even experts need much more distance to stop and crashes are more severe.

probe.question: Can an expert driver safely exceed the limit in a crowded street?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, skill makes it safe.

misconceptions.root_belief: skill can override physical laws

misconceptions.statement: Speed limits exist only so police can collect fines.
misconceptions.why: Students see enforcement and fines more than the reason.
misconceptions.fix: Limits are set from how far a vehicle needs to stop and how many people, such as pedestrians, use that road.

probe.question: Why is there a 25 km/h limit near a school?
probe.wrong_answer: So that police can fine people.

misconceptions.root_belief: rules exist for authority's benefit, not safety

misconceptions.statement: When a driver presses the brake, the vehicle stops at once.
misconceptions.why: Students see braking as an instant action.
misconceptions.fix: The driver needs reaction time, and then the vehicle keeps moving during braking, so stopping takes extra distance.

probe.question: A child runs onto the road 5 m ahead of a car at 40 km/h. Will it stop in time?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the driver just brakes and it stops.

misconceptions.root_belief: changes happen instantly
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas of motion and stopping

misconceptions.statement: Brakes work equally well on dry and wet roads.
misconceptions.why: Students think brakes alone control stopping.
misconceptions.fix: Wet roads reduce friction, so tyres grip less and the stopping distance is longer.

probe.question: On a rainy day, does stopping distance change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, brakes work the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: one component alone determines the result
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on friction and motion misconceptions

misconceptions.statement: Anyone above 14 can drive any motorbike on public roads.
misconceptions.why: Students see underage riders on the road and assume it is allowed.
misconceptions.fix: The minimum age is generally 18; 16 is allowed only for gearless two-wheelers up to 50cc, with a licence.

probe.question: Can a 15-year-old drive a 100cc motorbike on the road?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if they can ride well.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is commonly seen is allowed

misconceptions.statement: A licence is needed only for cars, not for scooters or mopeds.
misconceptions.why: Smaller vehicles seem less serious.
misconceptions.fix: A licence is required for every motor vehicle on public roads, including scooters and mopeds.

probe.question: Does a 16-year-old on a low-power scooter need a licence?
probe.wrong_answer: No, scooters do not need one.

misconceptions.root_belief: smaller things need fewer rules

misconceptions.statement: Talking on the phone with hands-free is perfectly safe while driving.
misconceptions.why: Students think the only danger is holding the phone.
misconceptions.fix: Hands-free talking still distracts the mind and slows reactions; it is safer not to use a phone while driving.

probe.question: A driver uses a hands-free headset. Is the risk gone?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both hands are on the wheel.

misconceptions.root_belief: only physical actions matter, not attention

misconceptions.statement: A little alcohol makes a driver more relaxed and careful.
misconceptions.why: Alcohol is believed to calm people.
misconceptions.fix: Alcohol slows reactions and weakens judgement even in small amounts; drinking and driving is a crime.

probe.question: Does one drink improve driving?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it makes the driver calmer.

misconceptions.root_belief: a feeling of control means better control
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO road safety reports on drink-driving
